approved: Defence Amendment (Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence) Bill 2025
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would create a new parliamentary committee to oversee Australia's defence agencies.
The committee would have up to 13 members and could request information, documents, and briefings, but would be restricted from publicly disclosing sensitive information without ministerial approval.
The bill includes criminal offences for unauthorised use or disclosure of protected information by committee members, their staff, and other authorised parliamentarians.
Creates the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence within the Defence Act 1903.
Gives the committee power to review, monitor, and report on Australian defence agencies, excluding certain intelligence organisations.
Imposes restrictions on public proceedings and disclosure of protected information, with ministerial certificates overriding disclosure requirements.
Establishes criminal offences for unauthorised use or disclosure of protected information.

Australian defence agencies, including the Australian Defence Force, Department of Defence, and Department of Veterans' Affairs, as well as committee members, their staff, and other authorised parliamentarians.

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2026-02-05.46.2) to agree with the bill's main idea. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill for a second time. This means they can now discuss the bill in greater detail. ### What does this bill do? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2526/26bd023), which is a document put together by the parliamentary library: > *The security situation in the Indo–Pacific region is challenging and deteriorating. Australian defence spending and activity is increasing in response. Due to security risks, an increasing number of defence matters cannot be properly scrutinised in public hearings of the Joint Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade (JSCFADT).* > > *The Defence Amendment (Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence) Bill 2025 (the Bill) proposes a Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence (the Committee), to take on JSCFADT’s Defence-related functions. The Committee is modelled on the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security (PJCIS).* > > *A Bill in very similar terms, the Defence Amendment (Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence) Bill 2024 (the 2024 Bill), was introduced to the 47th Parliament but negatived at third reading in the Senate. Despite proposal of a number of amendments, consensus could not be reached on Committee membership.* > > *There are very few changes from the 2024 Bill and those changes are technical rather than substantive. In particular, the membership provisions are unchanged.* > > *At the time of writing, the Bill had not been referred to or reported on by any parliamentary committees. However, the 2024 Bill was considered by the Senate Scrutiny of Bills Committee and the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Human Rights.
